summary: LunaLight is a web app that helps mission planners compare lunar landing sites in seconds. Missions to the Moon’s South Pole face extreme conditions: the Sun never rises above about 1.5 degrees, ridges cast huge shadows, and Earth hangs on the horizon where terrain can block communication. Existing tools like JPL Horizons, Quickmap and Moon Trek are powerful but too complex for quick comparison. LunaLight shows three sites side by side, each with a sky dome that places the Sun and Earth by azimuth and elevation, six key metrics (power %, sunlight duration, Earth visibility window and more), and a clear GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict. A timeline shows sunrise and sunset across the 29.53-day lunar day, so planners can pick the right site and date at a glance. An Education Mode explains the science for the public.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

LunaLight is a frontend web app for quick comparison of lunar landing sites. For any site and date it shows where the Sun and Earth are in the lunar sky and returns a GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict for solar power and direct-to-Earth communication.

THE PROBLEM

At the Moon's South Pole the Sun never rises more than about 1.5 degrees above the horizon, so terrain creates long shadows and long dark periods. Earth is nearly fixed in the sky (tidal locking), sits close to the horizon near the pole, and wobbles by about +/-2 degrees (libration), so a ridge can cut the communication link. Tools like JPL Horizons, Quickmap and Moon Trek are powerful but too complex for rapid comparison.

HOW IT WORKS

- Choose up to three sites (Shackleton Crater Rim, Malapert Massif, Nobile Crater, de Gerlache Crater, Apollo 11, or custom latitude/longitude), a date, and a position within the 29.53-day lunar day.

- Each site card has a sky dome showing the Sun and Earth by azimuth and elevation, with the local terrain horizon. Bodies below the horizon or behind terrain are dimmed.

- Six metrics per site: solar elevation, Earth elevation, sunlight duration, Earth visibility window, power generation %, and time remaining before sunset.

- Verdict: GO if the Sun and Earth are both above the horizon, CAUTION if only the Sun is, NO-GO if the Sun is below the horizon.

- A timeline chart shows Sun elevation (or power %) over 29.53 days with sunrise and sunset markers.

- Education Mode explains the science in plain English.

METHOD

A simplified ephemeris model: 29.53-day synodic period, 1.54-degree axial tilt, tidal locking with a +/-2 degree libration wobble. Sun and Earth directions are converted to azimuth and elevation for each site using 3D vector geometry. A parameterized terrain mask stands in for real horizon data. Power % is based on the sine of solar elevation.

IMPACT

Faster early-stage site screening for CLPS-style missions, a tool a non-technical decision-maker can read in 30 seconds, and a public education resource on why the lunar South Pole is so extreme.

TOOLS

React, Vite, Tailwind CSS and Recharts. Frontend only, no backend, deployed as a static site.

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

This MVP uses a simplified ephemeris and a stylized terrain mask, so it is for comparison and education, not flight operations. Next: the JPL Horizons API for exact ephemerides, LOLA elevation data for true horizon masking and shadows, more candidate sites, and a relay-satellite option for CAUTION sites.

USE OF AI

The application code and the text of this description were developed with assistance from Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant. The team directed the concept, requirements and design, and reviewed and tested the result. The app uses no AI at runtime and contains no AI-generated images, video or audio.
